cse-2007-cs-45.approach: Count work per call: apart from the recursive call each call does $O(1)$ work, so $T(n)=T(\sqrt n)+O(1)$. Substitute $n=2^m$ to turn the square root into halving.

steps.title: Write the recurrence
steps.body:
The addition $+\,n$ is a single $O(1)$ operation (it is the returned *value* that grows, not the work). Hence
$$T(n)=T(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor)+c,\qquad T(n)=1 \text{ for } n\le 2.$$

steps.title: Substitute $n=2^m$
steps.body:
Let $S(m)=T(2^m)$. Since $\sqrt{2^m}=2^{m/2}$,
$$S(m)=S(m/2)+c \Rightarrow S(m)=\Theta(\log_2 m).$$

steps.title: Back-substitute
steps.body:
$m=\log_2 n$, so $T(n)=\Theta(\log_2 m)=\Theta(\log_2\log_2 n)$.

Example: $n=2^{16}=65536 \to 256 \to 16 \to 4 \to 2$: 4 recursive calls, and $\log_2\log_2 65536=\log_2 16=4$.

animation.title: Calls for n = 65536
animation.caption: Each call halves log₂ n, so the depth is log₂ log₂ n.

optionAnalysis.reason: $\Theta(n^2)$ is far too large; there is no loop and only one recursive call per level.
$\Theta(n\log n)$ would need linear work per level; each level does constant work.
$\Theta(\log n)$ is the depth if the argument were halved ($n/2$); the square root halves the *exponent*, giving far fewer levels.
Correct: the depth of repeated square roots is $\log_2\log_2 n$, with $O(1)$ work per level.

cse-2007-cs-47.approach: The leaf-to-root path in a heap has $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$ nodes and is already sorted, so binary search on it costs $\log_2$ of the path length.

steps.title: Length of the path
steps.body: A heap with $n$ elements is a complete binary tree of height $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, so the path from the new leaf to the root has $k=\Theta(\log_2 n)$ nodes.

steps.title: The path is sorted
steps.body: In a max-heap each parent $\ge$ child, so the keys along the leaf→root path are in non-decreasing order. Their array indices $i,\lfloor i/2\rfloor,\lfloor i/4\rfloor,\dots$ are computable in $O(1)$, so binary search applies.

steps.title: Count comparisons
steps.body: Binary search on $k$ sorted items takes $\Theta(\log_2 k)=\Theta(\log_2\log_2 n)$ comparisons. (Shifting elements still costs $\Theta(\log n)$ moves, but the question asks only for comparisons.)

cse-2007-cs-53.approach: Give a regular grammar that is not LL(1) to kill P; for Q, note every regular language is deterministic context-free, and every DCFL has an LR(1) grammar.

steps.title: P is false

cse-2007-cs-54.approach: Evaluate the deepest subexpression first so that each result stays in a register: compute $t_3=e-(c+d)$ in R1, $t_1$ in R2, combine with a register-register SUB, and store once. Only loads of the first operand and the final store need MOV.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: Any OP leaves its result in a register, and the final value must reach memory, so at least $1$ store MOV is needed. Each of the two independent chains ($a+b$ and $e-(c+d)$) needs a first operand loaded into a register: $\ge 2$ load MOVs. So at least $3$.

steps.title: Code with 3 MOVs
steps.body:
| # | Instruction | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | MOV c, R1 | $R1=c$ |
| 2 | ADD d, R1 | $R1=d+c=t_2$ |
| 3 | SUB e, R1 | $R1=e-t_2=t_3$ |
| 4 | MOV a, R2 | $R2=a$ |
| 5 | ADD b, R2 | $R2=b+a=t_1$ |
| 6 | SUB R2, R1 | $R1=R2-R1=t_1-t_3=t_4$ |
| 7 | MOV R1, m | memory $\leftarrow t_4$ |

`OP m,Ri` computes *val* OP Ri, so `SUB e, R1` gives $e-t_2$ in the right order, and `SUB R2, R1` gives $R2-R1=t_1-t_3$.

cse-2007-cs-64.approach: Draw the precedence graph of each schedule from conflicting pairs (same item, different transactions, at least one write); a cycle means not conflict serializable.

steps.title: S1 conflicts
steps.body:
$S_1: r_1(X)\,r_1(Y)\,r_2(X)\,r_2(Y)\,w_2(Y)\,w_1(X)$
- $r_1(Y)$ before $w_2(Y)$ → $T_1\to T_2$.
- $r_2(X)$ before $w_1(X)$ → $T_2\to T_1$.

Cycle $T_1\to T_2\to T_1$: **not** conflict serializable.

steps.title: S2 conflicts
steps.body:
$S_2: r_1(X)\,r_2(X)\,r_2(Y)\,w_2(Y)\,r_1(Y)\,w_1(X)$
- $r_2(X)$ before $w_1(X)$ → $T_2\to T_1$.
- $w_2(Y)$ before $r_1(Y)$ → $T_2\to T_1$.
- $r_1(X)$, $r_2(X)$ — read/read, no conflict.

Only edges $T_2\to T_1$: acyclic, equivalent to serial $T_2,T_1$.

scene.title: Precedence graph of S2
scene.caption: S2: acyclic → serial order T2, T1

answer.value: $S_1$ is not conflict serializable and $S_2$ is — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: $S_1$ has the cycle $T_1\to T_2\to T_1$.
Reversed: S1 is the non-serializable one.
Correct.
$S_2$ is conflict-equivalent to the serial schedule $T_2,T_1$.

cse-2007-cs-64.verification: Reordered $S_2$ by swapping non-conflicting adjacent operations into $r_2(X)r_2(Y)w_2(Y)r_1(X)r_1(Y)w_1(X)$ — a serial $T_2T_1$ schedule.

cse-2007-cs-65.approach: Exactly one transmitter: choose which station ($n$ ways), it transmits ($p$), the other $n-1$ stay silent ($(1-p)^{n-1}$).

steps.title: One specific station
steps.body: $P(\text{station } i \text{ alone})=p(1-p)^{n-1}$.

steps.title: Any one station
steps.body:
These $n$ events are disjoint, so
$$P=\binom n1 p(1-p)^{n-1}=np(1-p)^{n-1}.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: binomial probability of exactly one success in n trials.
Only says the other n − 1 are silent; it omits that one station transmits and the choice of station.
Probability that one *particular* station is the sole transmitter; misses the factor n.
Probability that at least one of n − 1 stations transmits — unrelated.

cse-2007-cs-65.verification: $n=2,\ p=\tfrac12$: exactly one of two transmits with probability $\tfrac12$; formula (A) gives $2\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac12$.

cse-2007-cs-66.approach: One bit time $=1/\text{bit rate}$; the equivalent cable length is the distance the signal travels in that time.

steps.title: Distance
steps.body: $$d=200\ \tfrac{\text{m}}{\mu\text{s}}\times0.1\ \mu\text{s}=20\ \text{m}.$$

optionAnalysis.reason: 500 m would need a 2.5 µs bit time (0.4 Mbps).
200 m is the distance covered in 1 µs, i.e. at 1 Mbps.
Correct: 200 m/µs × 0.1 µs.
50 m would correspond to 0.25 µs per bit (4 Mbps).
